Now deliver final answer.<|end_think|>**Step 1 – Range of squares**

A 6‑digit integer lies between \(100000\) and \(999999\).

\[
\sqrt{100000}\approx 316.23,\qquad \sqrt{999999}\approx 999.999
\]

Hence any 6‑digit perfect square must be \(n^{2}\) with  

\[
317\le n\le 999 .
\]

**Step 2 – Two‑digit perfect squares that contain no 0**

The two‑digit substrings must themselves be perfect squares and the whole number may not contain the digit \(0\).  
The two‑digit perfect squares are  

\[
16,\;25,\;36,\;49,\;64,\;81 .
\]

(01,04,09 contain a 0 and are therefore excluded.)

Thus each of the three 2‑digit blocks of the 6‑digit number must be one of the six values above.

**Step 3 – Forming candidates**

All possible candidates are obtained by concatenating three of the six blocks:

\[
\text{candidate}= \text{AB}\,\text{CD}\,\text{EF},
\qquad 
\text{AB},\text{CD},\text{EF}\in\{16,25,36,49,64,81\}.
\]

There are at most \(6^{3}=216\) such numbers.

**Step 4 – Testing which candidates are perfect squares**

Checking each integer \(n\) from 317 to 999 (i.e. each of the 683 squares) and keeping only those whose
decimal representation meets the block condition gives:

\[
\begin{aligned}
408^{2} &= 166\,464 &&\text{blocks } 16|64|64,\\[2pt]
804^{2} &= 646\,416 &&\text{blocks } 64|64|16 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Both contain no digit \(0\) and each block is one of the allowed two‑digit squares.

No other square in the list satisfies the three‐block condition.

**Step 5 – Count**

Thus exactly two six‑digit integers satisfy all three requirements.
